newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala announces sweeping privatization plan.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala announces sweeping privatization plan.

text.p: Guatemala's state-owned railway, telecommunications, electricity, post office, tourism office and airports will be sold or drastically restructured this year, the government's privatization czar said Thursday.
"The ambitious plan is to do as much as possible this year," Gustavo Saravia told reporters at a news conference.
Saravia said the government planned to grant concessions for the administration of ports, airports and the post office, open up the telecommunications market and sell stock in the telephone company.
It also plans to sell electricity plants and open up the energy market and sell railway concessions.

The privatization efforts are part of a larger state modernization program, which Saravia said includes deregulation, simplification of laws, decentralization of services and training programs for civil servants.
President Alvaro Arzu has also promised to modernize tax collection, the court system and state finances.
State modernization, but not privatization specifically, is among promises made in a historic treaty signed with leftist rebels on December 29.

In January, Guatemala received pledges of $1.9 billion in aid over four years from international donors and lenders to help foot the bill for peace programs, including the state modernization efforts.
Many of the privatization plans are already underway. The government plans to finance 10 percent of its 1997 budget by selling stock in Guatel, the state-owned telephone company.
The government will begin accepting bids next week for railway concessions and a French company has already been contracted to administer the post office.
Late last year, the Guatemalan legislature passed laws opening up the telecommunications and energy industries, but the latter has not gone into effect because of a court challenge.
Saravia said the government hoped to gain public support for privatization so the program would not be held up by worker protests or court battles.
"I hope the majority of Gautemalans support the process and agree so we can overcome these obstacles and achieve approval in the courts, congress and all the legal bodies," Saravia said.
